'''Michael Christopher Wendl''' is a mathematician and biomedical engineer who has worked on [[DNA sequencing theory]],<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Dorman | first1 = N | year = 2006 | title = The long and short of it | url = | journal = [[BioTechniques]] | volume = 41 | issue = 4| page = 367 }}</ref> covering and matching problems in probability, theoretical fluid mechanics, and co-wrote [[Phred base calling|Phred]].<ref>{{cite journal | url = http://genome.cshlp.org/content/8/3/175.long | pmid = 9521921 | volume=8 | issue=3 | title=Base-calling of automated sequencer traces using phred. I. Accuracy assessment | date=March 1998 | journal=Genome Res. | pages=175–85  | last1 = Ewing | first1 = B | last2 = Hillier | first2 = L | last3 = Wendl | first3 = MC | last4 = Green | first4 = P | doi = 10.1101/gr.8.3.175 | doi-access = free }}</ref> He was a scientist on the [[Human Genome Project]] and has done bioinformatics and biostatistics work in cancer. Wendl is of ethnic German heritage and is the son of the aerospace engineer [[Michael J. Wendl]].<ref name = "hummel">P Hummel and N Fuhry: "Sackelhausen im Banat" Volume 3, published by Heimatsortsgemeinschaft Sackelhausen, Reutlingen FRG, 2007, pages 2236-2237.</ref>

==Research Work==

===Theoretical Fluid Mechanics===

The problem of low Reynolds number flow in the gap between 2 infinite cylinders, so-called [[Couette flow]], was solved in 1845 by [[George Gabriel Stokes|Stokes]].<ref>[[George Gabriel Stokes|G. G. Stokes]](1845) [https://archive.org/stream/mathphyspapers01stokrich#page/n119/mode/2up "On the theories of the internal friction of fluids in motion and of the equilibrium and motion of elastic solids", in ''Mathematical and Physical Papers'', pp. 102-104, Cambridge, UK: Cambridge University Press, 1880.]</ref> Wendl reported the generalization of this solution for finite-length cylinders,<ref name = "bordag"/><ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Wendl | first1 = MC | year = 1999 | title = General Solution for the Couette Flow Profile | url = https://journals.aps.org/pre/abstract/10.1103/PhysRevE.60.6192 | journal = [[Physical Review|Physical Review E]] | volume = 60 | issue = 5| pages = 6192–6194 | doi = 10.1103/PhysRevE.60.6192 }}</ref> which can actually be built for experimental work, in 1999, as a series of [[Bessel function|modified Bessel functions]] <math>I_1</math> and <math>K_1</math>. He also examined a variety of other low Reynolds number rotational devices and shear-driven devices, including a general form of the unsteady disk flow problem, for which the velocity profile is:<ref name = "disks">Wendl MC (2001) Mathematical analysis of coaxial disk cellular shear loading devices, Review of Scientific Instruments 72(11), 4212-4217.</ref>

<math>
u(r,z,t) = \Re\left(e^{i\sigma t}\left[\frac{r\cdot\sinh(1+i)\beta z}{\sinh(1+i)\beta \phi}\right] + \frac{2}{\phi}\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^j\cdot\alpha_j^2\cdot\sin(\alpha_j z)\cdot I_1\left(\sqrt{i R \sigma + \alpha_j^2} r\right)}{(i R \sigma + \alpha_j^2)\cdot I_1\left(\sqrt{i R \sigma + \alpha_j^2}\right)}\right)
</math>

where <math>\sigma</math>, <math>R</math>, <math>\beta</math>, and <math>\phi</math> are physical parameters, <math>\alpha_j</math> are eigen-values, and <math>(r, z, t)</math> are coordinates. This result united prior-published special cases for steady flow, infinite disks, etc.<ref name = "disks"/>

===Covering and Matching Problems in Probability===

Wendl examined a number of matching and covering problems in combinatorial probability, especially as these problems apply to molecular biology. He determined the distribution of match counts of pairs of integer [[multiset]]s in terms of [[Bell polynomials]],<ref name = "multiset">Wendl MC (2005) Probabilistic assessment of clone overlaps in DNA fingerprint mapping via a priori models, J. Comp. Biol. 12(3), 283-297.</ref> a problem directly relevant to [[Gene mapping|physical mapping of DNA]]. Prior to this, investigators had used a number of ad-hoc quantifiers, like the [[Sulston score]], which idealized match trials as being independent. His result for the [[Birthday problem|multiple-group birthday proposition]]<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Wendl | first1 = MC | year = 2003 | title = Collision probability between sets of random variables | url = | journal = Stat. Prob. Lett. | volume = 64 | issue = 3| pages = 249–254 | doi = 10.1016/S0167-7152(03)00168-8 }}</ref> solves various related "collision problems", e.g. some types of [[Peer-to-peer|P2P searching]].<ref>Hautakorpi, J and Schultz, G (2010) ''A Feasibility Study of an Arbitrary Search in Structured Peer-to-Peer Networks'', IEEE Computer Communications and Networks, Proc ICCCN, pp 1–8.</ref> He has also examined a variety of 1-dimensional covering problems (see review by [[Cyril Domb]]<ref>[[Cyril Domb]] (1989) ''Covering by random intervals and one-dimensional continuum percolation'', J. Stat. Phys. 55, 441-460.</ref>), generalizing the basic configuration to forms relevant to molecular biology.<ref>Wendl MC (2008) Random covering of multiple one-dimensional finite domains with an application to DNA sequencing, SIAM J. Appl. Math. 68(3), 890-905.</ref><ref>Wendl MC, Kota K, Weinstock GM, and Mitreva M (2013) Coverage theories for metagenomic DNA sequencing based on a generalization of Stevens' theorem, J. Math. Biol. 67(5), 1141-1161.</ref> His covering investigation of rare DNA variants with [[Richard K. Wilson]]<ref>Wendl MC and Wilson RK (2009) The theory of discovering rare variants via DNA sequencing, BMC Genomics 10 art. 485.</ref> played a role in designing the [[1000 Genomes Project]].<ref>Altshuler DM et al. (2010) A map of human genome variation from population-scale sequencing, Nature 467(7319), 1061-1073.</ref>

===Bioinformatics and Biostatistics===

Wendl co-wrote [[Phred base calling|Phred]], a widely used DNA trace analyzer that converted raw output stream of early DNA sequence machines to sequence strings.<ref>Koboldt, D. C. and Miller, R. D. (2011) ''Identification of Polymorphic Markers for Genetic Mapping'', chapter 2 in "Genomics: Essential Methods", John Wiley and Sons.</ref><ref>Highsmith, W. E. (2006) ''Electrophoretic Methods for Mutation Detection and DNA Sequencing'', chapter 9 in "Molecular Diagnostics for the Clinical Laboratorian", Humana Press</ref> He has contributed extensively to biostatistical analysis of cancer studies<ref>Lu C, Xie M, Wendl MC et al. (2015) Patterns and functional implications of rare germline variants across 12 cancer types, Nature Comm. 6 art. 10086.</ref><ref>Chen, F, Wendl MC, Wyczalkowski MA, Bailey MH, Li Y, and Ding, L (2015) Moving pan-cancer studies from basic research toward the clinic, Nature Cancer 2(9), 879-890.</ref> and to the bioinformatics toolbase,<ref>Wendl MC et al. (2011) PathScan: A tool for discerning mutational significance in groups of putative cancer genes, Bioinformatics 27(12), 1595-1602.</ref> collaborating frequently with [[Li Ding]], [[Elaine Mardis]], and [[Richard K. Wilson]].

==Personal life==
Wendl's heritage is ethnic German, originating from the [[Banat Swabians|Banat region]] of the old [[Austria-Hungary|Austro-Hungarian Empire]] and is a historian of [[Alpine folk music|Danube-Swabian folk music]].<ref>{{cite book|last=Rohr|first=Robert|date=1994|title=Unser Klingendes Erbe: Aus dem Musikleben der Donauschwaben von 1918 bis zur Gegenwart|location=Munich|publisher=Verlag der Donauschwaebische Kulturstiftung|volume=2|page=384}}</ref> He is the son of the aerospace engineer [[Michael J. Wendl]].<ref name = "hummel"/> He is married to the former Pamela Bjerkness of [[Chicago]]<ref>Hochzeitsglocken lauteten fur Pamela Marie and Michael Christopher Wendl, [https://idnc.library.illinois.edu/?a=d&d=EIN19951202-01&e=-------en-20--1--txt-txIN---------- Eintracht] 74(13), December 2, 1995, page 6.</ref>
